    Want to Sell an Agency? Launch a Creator Marketing Firm

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In recent months, the market for creator and social agencies has been, to put it lightly, brisk.
    • It has been revealed that in September, the Madrid-based social agency Samy acquired Get Engaged, a U.S.
    • In October, Billion Dollar Boy Group bought Creator Authority, a business-to-business influencer agency, and the private equity firm Shamrock Capital, which owns ADWEEK, made an eight-figure investment in the social-first agency Saylor.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In recent months, the market for creator and social agencies has been, to put it lightly, brisk.

    It has been revealed that in September, the Madrid-based social agency Samy acquired Get Engaged, a U.S. social and influencer shop, in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

    In October, Billion Dollar Boy Group bought Creator Authority, a business-to-business influencer agency, and the private equity firm Shamrock Capital, which owns ADWEEK, made an eight-figure investment in the social-first agency Saylor.

    It has been revealed that earlier this month, the social-first agency LV8 merged with its sister company Mirage Digital on the back of a “high eight figures” investment from Velocity Capital Management. And last week, the private equity firm Falfurrias Management Partners took a majority stake in Freeman & Forrest, another B2B creator agency.

    The deals are part of a record year, according to James Creech, founder of the creator M&A advisory firm Quartermast. There have been 30 agency acquisitions in the creator economy so far in 2026, up from 20 in all of 2025 and above the previous high of 28 in 2022, according to Quartermast data.

    Overall, there have been 124 M&A creator-adjacent deals this year, the busiest on record, and roughly half of the agency deals have come since July, per Quartermast.

    Behind the surge is a crop of boutiques founded during the pandemic-era influencer boom that have matured into businesses worth buying, which are run by founders who need more resources to keep up with what clients are asking for.

    Recent findings suggest that A specific set of firms—social-first creative shops, podcast agencies, TikTok Shop specialists, and B2B creator plays—are responsible for the majority of this interest, while the deals themselves are increasingly financed by a newly introduced cohort of buyers, including private equity firms, strategic roll-ups, and international firms. All of it is unfolding in a frothy market for creator economy deals, which is just now beginning to consolidate in response to urgent demand across a fragmented space.

    Recent findings suggest that “Creator marketing works,” Creech stated. “Brands and their agency partners are going to continue to invest there.”.

    The current rush of creator agency activity has its origins in the pandemic, according to LV8 chief executive Griffin Haddrill.

    Lockdown acted as a digital accelerant, pulling budgets toward creators at a moment when television and film had dried up and out-of-home advertising had stopped working.

    Because acquisitions typically take nine to 12 months to come together, the resulting deal volume spiked in 2021 and 2022, slowed over the following two years, and has since normalized, Creech said.

    Recent findings suggest that the same period produced a wave of new agencies, many of which were founded by executives who saw the emerging relevance of the creator ecosystem and debuted startups to service it. Five years later, those boutiques have matured into businesses worth buying, according to Haddrill.

    FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context.

    For founders, selling offers the resources to keep up with clients, according to Get Engaged co-founder Ben Hiott.

    “Social is becoming the center of how brands build their businesses, and clients are asking us to do more every year,” Hiott mentioned in October.

    The wave of dealmaking that followed the pandemic was primarily influencer agencies, according to Creech, while this year, the variety of targets has expanded.

    In 2026, buyers have gone after social-first creative agencies, such as Get Engaged, OK Cool, and Sway Social; podcast and audio shops like Ad Results Media and Listening Party Agency; and TikTok Shop specialists including Orca, Uptickk, and Yada.

    In a recent development, private equity is also getting more involved in the space, investing capital after years of financing strategic acquirers, as Bridgepoint does with Samy, according to Creech. This year, Shamrock Capital took a majority stake in Saylor, Velocity became a near-equal partner in LV8, and Falfurrias bought Freeman & Forrest, among other deals.

    In a recent development, serial acquirers are consolidating the field as well. Influencer agency Ykone has made four acquisitions in 2026, and creator company network Residence has made two, while Samy and Publicis remain active, according to Creech. After large platform deals for Influential and Captiv8, Publicis has turned to regional acquisitions, including the French creator agency Point d’Orgue, to enter new markets, according to Creech.

    For investors, the opportunity lies in stitching these shops together, according to Haddrill.

    “The consumer demand was there, but the agency space was fragmented,” Haddrill noted. “Now, investors are seeing this fragmentation and working to bring them together.”.

    B2B creator marketing has also emerged as its own category.

    Creator Authority, whose clients include Amazon, Adobe, and Mastercard, was Billion Dollar Boy Group’s first acquisition, an all-cash, multimillion-dollar deal with an earnout component, according to Business Insider.

    Freeman & Forrest, founded in 2024 by Emily Freeman and Forrest Brazeal after they ran influencer programs at Microsoft and Google Cloud, helps tech companies like Amazon and Google reach technical customers through creators.

    And more of the deals cross borders: Get Engaged gave Samy a U.S. base after the agency built its business in Europe and Latin America, and dealmaking between the U.S. and the U.K. has picked up in both directions, according to Creech.

    As the ecosystem matures, the next wave of dealmaking may come from the middle of the market, according to a creator management executive who asked not to be named.

    The largest independents, such as Whalar and Influential, have already sold to Accenture Song and Publicis, respectively, which leaves room for midsize independents, many of which will come to market over the next 12 months, the executive said.

    Creator management firms, which run creators’ businesses rather than simply booking their brand deals, are likely the next category to consolidate, the executive added.

    The buying, in other words, is far from over, according to Creech.

    According to recent reports, “It’s mature, it’s scaled, it’s professionalized. The work is not done,” Creech said. “We’re maybe entering middle innings.”.

    Sources indicate that hearst CMO Heads Out (SCOOP): The chief marketing officer at Hearst Magazines, Sherri Chambers, will be leaving the organization in a few weeks, according to sources. Chambers, who joined the digital media firm in December 2024, confirmed the news, while a Hearst Magazines spokesperson expressed their gratitude for Chambers in a statement. The departure is the latest in a series of executive shake-ups. In July, Hearst Magazines appointed Chris Berend as its first chief content and experience officer, and in October, it named A+E executive Juliana Stock as its new president, replacing Debi Chirichella, who will become chair of the group. The legacy media firm has worked hard to cultivate a reputation for calm and consistency in an otherwise turbulent industry, but it certainly looks as if the company is aiming to turn some kind of corner.

    Bunny Boss Bolts: The editor in chief of Playboy, Phillip Picardi, has left the organization after less than a year, Puck reported earlier this week. According to a company spokesperson, the move was a personal decision, with Picardi returning to Los Angeles after Playboy set up headquarters in—where else—Miami. But Picardi only began the job officially in March, meaning his tenure at the publisher only lasted a brief eight months. Given all the fanfare surrounding his appointment, I have to imagine something went seriously awry. Or Picardi, who did not return my request for comment, landed an otherwise irrefusable job elsewhere. This is disappointing because I liked the direction Playboy was heading under Picardi, reporting on the state of sex, dating, and relationships in this fraught moment—but maybe the loyal fanbase did not.

    BuzzFeed Taps Influential (EXCLUSIVE): On Monday, BuzzFeed named its first chief revenue officer under its upcoming ownership, tapping Chris Poydenis, co-founder of the creator marketing firm Influential, to lead its revenue division. The appointment comes as BuzzFeed attempts an ambitious shift in direction, positioning itself as a source of free, ad-supported television, bundled with the rest of the Allen Media Group portfolio. The decision to name a creator marketing executive as the chief sales lead clearly telegraphs the manner in which BuzzFeed would like to evolve, shifting focus to its creators and video franchise talent. Will it work? The odds are long.

    Sara Kehaulani Goo is president of The Washington Post’s creator network, a latest division that sits outside of the newsroom and makes sponsored short-form video series with independent creators. Goo, formerly the editor in chief of Axios, launched the first show in April, and the network has since released six series in categories ranging from personal finance to career advice.

    Sources indicate that publishers increasingly want to work with creators, but the harder question is why creators would want to work with publishers. In our conversation, Goo and I discussed how The Post’s model works, why its creator content goes through Post fact-checking, and what a media manufacturer can offer talent who could go it alone.

    This interview has been edited.

    According to recent reports, mark Stenberg: You specifically left Axios to head up this latest creator division. Can you tell me about the role and how The Post is working with creators?

    Sara Kehaulani Goo: I spent 12 years of my career at The Post as a reporter and editor, so it’s been nice to return in a very different role. The theory is simple: Look at where people spend their time, where they get information, where trust is growing, and where revenue is growing across media. The answer to all of those questions is creators. So, we are working with knowledge creators, people who have built big audiences around their expertise, and treating them as equal editorial and business partners.

    Mark: How does a show actually work?

    Sara: We mostly work with creators who’ve built audiences with short-form video in lifestyle topics like personal finance, health and wellness, and career advice. Then, we develop the indicates together and publish them together. Last week, we debuted Her Next Move with an executive recruiter based in Upcoming York. She posts a two-minute video to her audience of a million people as a collab with us, so it reaches both audiences. We amplify it on The Post’s social accounts and publish it on our website and app. That show is sponsored by Uber.

    In a recent development, mark: Why would a creator want to work with the Post? Do they share in the revenue?

    In a recent development, sara: I won’t get into the details, but we pay them for their time. It’s similar to a contributor model, though not exactly like freelancing, because they’re entrepreneurs. A lot of them want to focus on the content, which is what journalists want too. We help build the business around them, and we provide distribution and editorial support when they need it.

    Mark: Does their content go through Post fact-checking?

    Sources indicate that sara: Yes, through my team. The standards are the same. There’s a lack of consistency in the creator world when it comes to disclosing sponsorships, and to quality in general, and we can bring that. Trust in creators is growing, but people still wonder whether they should trust what they’re watching on Instagram and who paid for it. We can help answer that.

    Mark: It’s early, but how major is this now, and where is it headed?

    Industry observers note that sara: This year has been a proof of concept. We’ve done six shows with six creators, across health and wellness, personal finance, travel, career advice, and entertainment. Now we’re deciding which ones to renew, and next year we want to do more always-on content. Brands are very interested, because every brand is thinking about its creator strategy, and finding the right creator takes a lot of effort. We take that headache off their shoulders.

    Recent findings suggest that mark: Creators often relish operating on their own. How do you convince them to work with you?

    According to recent reports, sara: Having led newsrooms, I’ve always seen my job as spotting talent, developing it, and creating an environment where people can do their best work. This is the same. Creators are entrepreneurs, and the platforms give them plenty of ways to make money on their own. But being an entrepreneur isn’t for everybody, at least not at every level. Media companies have always worked with outside experts. The structure just looks different now.

    5 Black Friday Truths About Gen Z Shoppers and the Mall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to Black Friday—the start of the most critical five days of the year for retail brands.
    • According to Circana, 43% of Americans will do most of their holiday shopping between today and Monday, and nearly a quarter of them will do most of it today, full stop.
    • This is also the day that brands are focused on Gen Z, because 94% of them strategy to shop this week, according to Deloitte, and they’ll spend an average of $752—more than any other age cohort.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to Black Friday—the start of the most critical five days of the year for retail brands.

    According to Circana, 43% of Americans will do most of their holiday shopping between today and Monday, and nearly a quarter of them will do most of it today, full stop.

    This is also the day that brands are focused on Gen Z, because 94% of them strategy to shop this week, according to Deloitte, and they’ll spend an average of $752—more than any other age cohort.

    According to recent reports, it’s a given that many consumers aged 14-29 will spend that money online. But a lot of shopping is also going to happen at the place Gen X made famous: the mall.

    It has been revealed that you’ll find plenty of zoomers in malls today, in fact, but they’re not all spending the way you think, and some aren’t there to shop at all. ADWEEK waded through a stack of recent market studies and tapped the shoulders of a few experts to plumb Gen Z’s current relationship with the mall and what it means for Black Friday 2026.

    Gen X might have been the original mall rats in the 1980s, but today’s 18-29 age group has picked up the mantle.

    According to Coresight research released in April, 48% of Gen Z consumers say they’ve hit the mall in the last two weeks. A recent Ipsos survey found that shoppers aged 18-34 were twice as likely as those 55 and up to shop at the mall. And according to a Stagwell study released this year, Gen Z not only spends more time at the mall on a per-visit basis, they also spend $296 per visit on average, the most of any age group.

    According to recent reports, gen Z mall affinity seems strongest with women, too. A 2026 study of female zoomers’ shopping activity conducted by snack maker Sunnie and Westfield Rise found that 86% of them praised the mall for giving them “energy they can’t get digitally.”.

    The reasons why Gen Z likes the mall have as much to do with what the mall is as what it’s not—a small screen. Mall shopping represents a rebound effect in retail form, a response to hours of isolated scrolling.

    According to recent reports, coresight’s work states it plainly. “Gen Z has grown up with frictionless digital commerce as a baseline expectation,” researchers wrote, “yet precisely because of this ubiquity, they increasingly seek the tangible, social and experiential dimensions of physical retail.”.

    It’s worth noting that experts are also starting to see the same dynamic unfolding with Gen Alpha (aged 13 and under), whose spending power and influence is already approaching $100 billion, per Charles Schwab.

    “A trip to the mall with friends can be an notable first taste of autonomy,” Helenor Gilmour, head of marketing research firm Beano Brain, told ADWEEK. “That shared experience is a powerful part of the appeal of shopping in stores. It is why we expect younger shoppers to embrace shopping events like Black Friday as a reason to visit malls together.”.

    It has been revealed that brieane Olson, CEO of PacSun, is well positioned to observe the evolving shopping habits of Gen Z. The brand sells its apparel online, in freestanding stores, and at mall locations. It’s easy to assume that a generation that grew up with ecommerce would stick to what they know; or they might defect because they’re tired of it. But the truth lay in between.

    It has been revealed that “We’re continuing to see just how important physical retail is to young consumers, and there’s a real opportunity for malls heading into Black Friday and the holiday season,” Olson told ADWEEK. “Young people aren’t choosing between digital and physical experiences. They want both, and they expect brands to create meaningful connections across each.”.

    With over 520 stores across 4.2 million square feet and sales north of $650 million a year, Bloomington, Minnesota’s Mall of America (MOA) is the biggest mall in the continental U.S. According to its 2026 Holiday Shopping Survey, 92% of Gen Z respondents expressed an intent to show up there today, with over half saying they planned to spend once they arrive.

    Just as significantly, MOA has charted a symbiotic relationship between the online culture Gen Z consumes and their behavior when they visit.

    According to recent reports, “Social media may introduce them to a brand, trend or community, but there’s still an appeal to experiencing those interests firsthand,” noted a MOA spokesperson. “We’re seeing that with our leasing strategy. Brands such as Edikted and Pop Mart, along with concepts like Bandai Namco and Kpop Nara, reflect how interests that develop online are translating into physical retail experiences.”.

    “Gen Z may discover what’s next online,” MOA chief business development and marketing officer Jill Renslow added, “but they still want to experience it together in the real world.”.

    From a brand perspective, it’s not enough that Gen Z merely visits the mall—retailers still need to woo them once they get there.

    According to the International Council of Shopping Centers, 60% of Gen Z mall visitors say they go “just to socialize or meet friends.” Sunnie and Westfield North’s work found that 72% of female zoomers would still visit the mall even if it meant they couldn’t buy anything.

    It has been revealed that but there’s still a marketing opportunity here. Coresight’s study determined that social-media content creation is a big reason for mall visits, calling them “aesthetically curated spaces [that] serve as backdrops for organic and shareable moments.”.

    The brands that benefit most, mentioned the study, are those that boast “visually engaging environments with Instagrammable decor.”.

    Robert Klara is the senior editor of brands at Adweek, specializing in the evolution and impact of brands.

    #159478. Tech Report: Show Your Work: Platforms Must Make Safety Decisions That Brands Can Verify

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1448 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adweek ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Show Your Work: Platforms Must Make Safety Decisions That Brands Can Verify

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This column is adapted from the keynote address that X Head of Safety Michael O’Herlihy gave at the recent Brand and AI Safety Summit.
    • Recent findings suggest that when I was at school in Ireland, math exams had a rule I thought was deeply unfair.
    • However, if you showed your work, and your method was right but you’d slipped on one line, you still got partial credit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This column is adapted from the keynote address that X Head of Safety Michael O’Herlihy gave at the recent Brand and AI Safety Summit.

    Recent findings suggest that when I was at school in Ireland, math exams had a rule I thought was deeply unfair. You were allowed to just write down the answer—but if the answer was wrong, you got nothing. Zero.

    However, if you showed your work, and your method was right but you’d slipped on one line, you still got partial credit.

    Sources indicate that it took me years to see the point. Showing your work doesn’t just give people an answer. It helps them understand how you got there. An answer on its own asks for trust; showing the work lets you check it.

    I’ve spent two decades in the business of judgment calls: what stays up, what comes down, what is eligible for reach. Every one of those judgments is an answer. And for most of that time, our industry has handed people the answer and kept the work hidden. For too long, this has been a black box.

    People ask me who makes better calls, humans or machines. Both make mistakes. If you give the same post to a hundred trained reviewers, you won’t get a hundred identical answers. So “human or machine?” is the wrong question. The right one is: Can you see the work?

    Today, mostly, you can’t see inside. The systems that decide what you see, and what sits next to an ad, run out of sight. The deal was “trust us.” It held while volumes were manageable, and it stopped working as they grew.

    Industry observers note that here’s the good news. AI doesn’t just make decisions faster. It gives us new ways to make those decisions explainable and testable. We now have the opportunity to turn the black box into a glass box: decisions you can trace back to the rules, and people outside who can check them, challenge them and help us improve them.

    But a glass box alone doesn’t make a system safe. You could fill one with bad decisions. It would just let people see them. So transparency on its own isn’t the standard—defensibility is. Can this decision be justified under the rules? Transparency provides the evidence: Can someone see how we got there? Verification is the test: Can someone outside check whether the system consistently follows the rules?

    Before returning to X, I worked at Reddit, where my colleague Rosa Català and I published a paper earlier this year called Escaping the Agreement Trap: Defensibility Signals for Evaluating Rule-Governed AI.

    The usual test for a content-decision system is whether it agreed with a human. Same answer, pass. Different answer, fail. We looked at more than 193,000 real content decisions from Reddit and asked whether each one could be traced back to the written rules.

    In a recent development, when the model and the human disagreed, the usual assumption is that the model got it wrong. But roughly four out of five of those model decisions could still be defended under the written rules. Disagreement doesn’t necessarily mean the model was wrong. Often, both opposing decisions were defensible. Grading by agreement is the wrong exam entirely: checking the answer, never the working.

    How can two opposite decisions both be defensible? Ambiguity. Two reasonable people can look at the same case, reach opposite conclusions, and both be within the rules. Some ambiguity isn’t a bug, it’s what happens when real people apply rules to real life. But a lot of it can be managed, and it starts with more detailed rules. When we gave the model detailed written rules instead of just bullets, measured ambiguity dropped from 18% to 7%.

    Sources indicate that so how do we actually build the glass box? One window at a time.

    It has been revealed that window one: See how it’s ranked. We open-sourced the For You algorithm, the system behind the feed: ranking, filtering and visibility-limiting labels. It’s on GitHub, and we keep it updated to match what’s running on X. Anyone can read it; you get the code, not a blog post about the code.

    Industry observers note that window two: Add context. That’s Community Notes, where contributors can add context to any post. A note is only shown publicly if enough contributors from different points of view rate it helpful. The algorithm is open, and so is the data. Context comes from the community, not from us.

    Window three: See what applies to your account. My colleague Keith Coleman’s team built Under the Hood. It shows account holders the visibility decisions that apply to them, and any restrictions applied due to a government request or court order. You don’t have to guess. You can look.

    Sources indicate that window four: Understand the decision. This is what we’re building in Safety. Not just making decisions visible, but giving people clear ways to understand them, challenge them and help us get them right. When we label a post, the author will be able to tap the label and see what it was based on, in plain language, not code or model internals. They’ll see what it means for reach: who it won’t be recommended to, and who will see it behind a warning. And they’ll be able to appeal, telling us what we should have seen, so we can take another look and fix it if we got it wrong.

    It has been revealed that sometimes people will still disagree, and that’s fine. Agreement was never the goal. What we want to hear is, “I still disagree, but I see why you got there.” A mistake you can see is a mistake you can fix. But there is a limit.

    In a recent development, the glass box reveals the rules and the decisions, not the answer key. We don’t publish the signals and thresholds we use to catch spam, scams and coordinated abuse. Open enough to verify. Closed enough that it can’t be gamed.

    Sources indicate that the past few years have tested advertiser confidence across the industry, and no platform, including X, is exempt from that scrutiny. That skepticism is legitimate, and the right response isn’t to ask for trust back. It’s to make trust earnable. Brands need to understand the decisions that shape where their ads appear, because what’s allowed on a platform and what you want next to your ad are two different standards.

    Industry observers note that the X platform philosophy of “Freedom of Speech, Not Reach” is built on that distinction. Lawful speech can stay up without being amplified. But limited reach should never mean hidden decisions.

    Recent findings suggest that our rules decide what’s allowed; ranking decides what we recommend. Suitability decides what sits next to a brand, and that’s the brand’s call, not ours. Every brand draws that line differently; advertisers shouldn’t have to accept someone else’s definition of what’s suitable for them.

    In a recent development, control means setting your own standard. Transparency means seeing where your ads appear. Independent measurement means verifying whether it’s working. Published rules tell you what should happen. Transparency highlights you what happened.

    But neither, on its own, proves that a system is working consistently at scale. Verification does. Platforms shouldn’t be the only ones grading their own work, which is why at X we partner with DoubleVerify and Integral Ad Science.

    Recent findings suggest that to the platforms: Show your work. Write rules clear enough that decisions can be traced back to them, and let people outside your walls check the results.

    Recent findings suggest that to brands and agencies: Ask for it. Make “Can I check this?” a normal question, and ask every platform, including X: Can I set my own suitability standard? Can I see where my ads actually ran? Who outside your firm checks it? Safety shouldn’t be something platforms ask you to trust. It should be something you can verify.

    It has been revealed that those math exams had it right. Showing your work gives people the confidence to understand how you got there, and when you get it wrong, it gives them the evidence to say so.

    “Trust us” belongs to the black box. It’s time to build the glass box. Show your work.

    According to recent reports, michael O'Herlihy is Head of Safety at X, where he leads the work to keep people safe across the platform and its AI systems while protecting free expression and increasing transparency. He has more than two decades of senior leadership experience in technology, safety, product, and incident response, including roles at Google, Uber, Meta, Reddit, and X.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clutch helps credit unions launch digital lending and account opening. As a Senior Implementation Engineer, you're the product specialist who solves the hardest technical problems on those projects.

    You specialize in one Clutch product and cross-train on a second. You join each project at key moments and whenever it needs something beyond the default setup. An Engagement Manager owns each project and the relationship with the credit union.

    This role fits someone who can diagnose a complicated setup, explain it to a non-technical audience and decide when a request is worth building.

    Diagnose complicated setups and find working answers through configuration, mapping, integration design and workarounds.

    Design and build non-standard configuration, core mapping and integrations.

    Decide whether a requested change is worth making. When it isn't, say no, explain why and offer an alternative.

    Own the testing strategy and lead live testing sessions with credit union teams.

    In a recent development, advise our implementation team on what's possible, what needs a workaround and what's a true product gap. File clear tickets with our product and engineering teams for the gaps.

    Help write and improve our best-practice default setup, workbooks and test scripts with our Product and Engineering teams.

    Coach Engagement Managers to run standard setup themselves.

    Use AI to speed up your work, and standardize what works with the team.

    Work on many projects at once. Occasional onsite visits with customers.

    Recent findings suggest that our Professional Services team implements Clutch for our credit union customers. Every project starts from a best-practice default, and we change it when the change improves the credit union's outcome. We test the setup with the credit union and take them live. Our top metric is customer success through renewal and expansion. We look for people with high agency, sound judgment and a strong technical foundation, who keep teammates informed.

    According to recent reports, our firm is growing quickly, and so is our team. We're looking for people who want to help shape a world-class delivery motion.

    Learn our default setups, decision log and the core and vendor systems around your product.

    Join your first projects alongside a tenured Implementation Engineer.

    Complete onboarding and lead the technical design on several projects.

    Handle your first non-standard configurations and integrations on your own.

    Be the go-to person for your product area.

    Contribute to our default setups, workbooks and test scripts.

    Coach Engagement Managers on standard setup.

    5+ years of experience in implementation, solutions engineering or technical consulting, ideally in fintech or banking software.

    According to recent reports, 2+ years integrating with web APIs. You read and write code (Python, JSON, JavaScript or similar), work comfortably in GitHub and the terminal, and debug payloads yourself.

    A record of diagnosing complex setups and finding working answers without engineering work.

    Sound judgment on which changes are worth making, and the confidence to say no and explain why.

    A grasp of why a product works the way it does and what it does for a customer's business.

    A named result from using AI in your work, such as time saved or a faster diagnosis.

    It has been revealed that comfort with ambiguity. You build a plan, tracker or checklist when none exists.

    The ability to explain technical concepts clearly to non-technical audiences.

    You communicate proactively. You flag risks early and keep Engagement Managers and customers informed.

    The ability to keep many projects moving in the same week.

    Experience with core banking or credit union core systems, Alloy, Stripe, Plaid or ACH.

    Please note that this role may evolve as our business needs change, so we appreciate your flexibility and adaptability.

    Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

    Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

    Paid Time Off: Enjoy flexible PTO days yearly for relaxation and rejuvenation.

    Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

    Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

    Health Coverage: Prioritize your well-being with comprehensive health and dental insurance looks.

    It has been revealed that clutch is a revolutionary vertical SaaS tech giant, proudly backed by Andreessen Horowitz (A16z), aimed at revolutionizing the way Credit Unions engage and change the lives of their members. As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

Please approach interviews without the use of AI tools—our goal is to get to know how you think, solve problems, and communicate. Once you're in the seat, bring on the prompts!

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that TRM Labs provides AI-powered intelligence solutions that help public and private sector agencies investigate and disrupt crime. TRM's platforms enable investigators to trace illicit activity, build cases, and construct operating pictures of threat networks. Leading agencies and businesses worldwide rely on TRM to make the world safer and more secure.

    Recent findings suggest that the Scam Investigations team is TRM’s tip of the spear against pig butchering syndicates, romance fraud networks, and investment scam operations that steal billions from victims each year. The team operates an integrated workflow — from AI-supported complaint triage to time-sensitive investigation, escalation, and recovery support for victims.

    In a recent development, as a Global Investigator, you will work at the recovery-focused layer of scam investigation. You will validate high-priority blockchain leads, conduct forward and backward tracing, assess whether funds touch regulated platforms or other actionable endpoints, and produce clear investigative documentation that supports time-sensitive escalation and victim-centered recovery outcomes.

    Support time-sensitive asset-preservation workflows with regulated platforms and ecosystem partners.

    Own the recovery side. After a freeze, run the backtrace that ties frozen funds to specific victims and produce the documentation that drives restitution. The freeze is the start. Victim recovery is the goal.

    Trace victim funds end-to-end — forward to the wallets that consolidate them, backward to the platforms they came from. Your work feeds directly into the legal packages that recover them.

    Validate time-sensitive blockchain signals and move high-confidence matters through the appropriate escalation workflow. Speed and accuracy both matter.

    Continuously learn newly introduced issues in crypto.

    Support other teams on time sensitive issues that might be unforeseen.

    React timely to the movement of funds during an ongoing investigation.

    Location / citizenship / clearance — placeholder, varies by region (NA seats: US Citizenship required, ability to obtain Public Trust clearance, US-based). EMEA / APAC seat requirements TBD by region.

    AI fluency (required) — you use AI tools in your workflow to synthesize returns, draft outputs, and accelerate analysis, with examples of how AI has impacted your work.

    According to recent reports, blockchain / cryptocurrency tracing (required, gating) — forward-then-backward trace, exchange attribution, co-mingling handling, multi-hop VASP tracing, and LIFO/FIFO backtrace for recovery work. Non-negotiable.

    Creative tactical thinking — demonstrated ability to pivot from a single point to a network view, identifying operators behind operations.

    Experience producing investigative packages that can support formal legal, compliance, or enforcement workflows.

    You think in outcomes, not lanes. If “that’s not what I was hired for” is a sentence you reach for, this isn’t the seat.

    You don’t need a checklist to start. Handed something you’ve never seen, you figure out the first move and take it. When the playbook stops, you keep going.

    3–5 years of cryptocurrency investigations or asset-recovery experience — law enforcement crypto units, blockchain analytics firms, exchange compliance investigations, or equivalent. You understand how regulated platforms behave under request, including the difference between voluntary cooperation and formal process, and you treat getting money back to victims as part of your job rather than a downstream handoff.

    Learn about TRM Speed in this position:.

    Surge availability expected during time-sensitive disruption windows.

    All output documented in Notion and TRM’s investigative tools.

    High autonomy, high standards, low bureaucracy — work directly with engineering, analysts, legal counterparts, and partners who depend on the team’s output.

    Distributed, async-first via Slack and Notion, with structured syncs for alignment.

    Follow-the-sun rotation — the team runs investigators across NA, EMEA, and APAC for around-the-clock coverage.

    Formal on-call rotation for high-priority events, such as hacks, law-enforcement support, and other time-sensitive matters.

    Weekly rotation, with occasional weekend coverage as needed.

    According to recent reports, if you’re interested in joining TRM, we encourage you to apply directly. Every application is reviewed by our Talent team.

    Recent findings suggest that before applying, review the job description carefully and highlight the experience and impact that best demonstrate the required qualifications. Please also provide thoughtful and accurate answers to the application questions, as these will be used to evaluate your skills and qualifications for the role.

    Recent findings suggest that if you send your resume directly to someone at TRM, we can’t guarantee it will reach the appropriate hiring team. Applying directly is the best way to ensure your application will be considered.

    Our process is designed to understand how you think, solve problems, and deliver impact, while allowing you to evaluate TRM. Most interview processes include a case study, an AI skills assessment, and a Leadership Principles interview.

    Recruiter Intro: Qualifications, motivations, and alignment with the role.

    Hiring Manager: Deep dive into your relevant experience, skills, and impact.

    First Round: 1–2 interviews focused on the skills most critical to the role.

    Final Round: Hands-on case study. This is usually a panel-style session where we go deeper into your craft, problem-solving, and alignment with TRM.

    References: Former colleagues who can provide insight into your work and impact.

    Offer: Congrats! Your recruiter will present the offer and compensation details.

    Welcome to TRM: We're excited to build a safer world with you!

    Your recruiter will share your specific interview proposal and preparation guidance along the way.

    AI fluency is a baseline expectation at TRM.

    We believe AI meaningfully changes how top performers operate. We expect every team member to use AI to accelerate and reimagine their craft, not just automate surface tasks.

    At TRM, AI fluency means you are among the top 10 percent of operators in your function in how you apply AI to:.

    Accelerate repeatable workflows.

    You will be evaluated on applied AI fluency during the interview process.

    We are building a safer world. That promise shows up in how we work every day.

    In a recent development, TRM moves FAST. We are a high-velocity, high-ownership team that expects clarity, follow-through, and impact. People who thrive here are energized by hard problems, experimentation, and continuous feedback. If something takes months elsewhere, it will ship here in days.

    Our work sits at the intersection of AI, national security, and fighting crime. The problems are complex, the stakes are real, and the environment evolves quickly. The pace and intensity of the work reflect the importance of the mission. As a result, the way we operate requires a high level of ownership, adaptability, collaboration, and creative problem-solving.

    Priorities and targets to change quickly.

    Operating with a high degree of ambiguity.

    A high level of personal ownership and accountability.

    Close collaboration across teams and functions.

    Frequent, high-touch communication.

    Creative problem-solving and out-of-the-box thinking.

    A pace that rewards urgency, adaptability, and outcomes.

    This environment is energizing for people who enjoy building, solving hard problems, and making progress in situations that are not always fully defined. It also requires thriving in ambiguity, adjusting course as fresh information emerges, and maintaining focus and positivity in a fast-moving and intense environment.

    We also recognize that this style of operating is not for everyone. If you are primarily optimizing for predictability or a consistently balanced workload, we encourage you to use the interview process to pressure-test whether this environment is truly the right fit. We want teammates who thrive here, not just survive here.

    If you are excited by meaningful problems, motivated by ambitious goals, and energized by working alongside mission-driven colleagues, there is a good chance you will find TRM to be an exceptional place to grow and contribute.

    Sources indicate that we hire and grow against three leadership principles. They’re the standards for how we operate, treat each other, and make decisions.

    It has been revealed that impact-Oriented Trailblazer: We put customers first and move with speed, focus, and adaptability. We treat every plan like an experiment – test, ship, measure, and iterate quickly.

    In a recent development, master Craftsperson: We care deeply about our craft. We balance speed with high standards, own outcomes end‑to‑end, and invest in getting better everyday.

    Recent findings suggest that inspiring Colleague: We add clarity and energy, not noise. We bring humility, candor, and a one‑team mindset — giving and receiving feedback to make the team stronger.

    At TRM, we care deeply about our craft. We are looking for individuals who want their work to matter, who experiment with speed and rigor, and who take pride in building a safer world for billions of people. If you’re excited by TRM’s mission but don’t check every box, we encourage you to apply — we hire for slope, judgment, and the will to learn fast.

Headquartered in San Francisco, TRM operates as a distributed-first company with hubs in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Latest York, Washington D.C., London, and Singapore.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Supabase runs millions of Postgres databases, and storage performance is now one of the biggest levers on how fast, reliable, and affordable they are.
    • As the senior engineer driving storage, you'll own this effort end to end: the architecture and build-vs-buy decisions, integration into our compute platform, and operating the system in production.
    • According to recent reports, your first goal is raw Postgres I/O performance at scale.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase runs millions of Postgres databases, and storage performance is now one of the biggest levers on how fast, reliable, and affordable they are. We're building a software-defined, NVMe-over-Fabrics storage platform underneath Supabase Postgres. Postgres stays unmodified, and the new layer delivers near-local-NVMe performance with the durability and flexibility of networked storage.

    As the senior engineer driving storage, you'll own this effort end to end: the architecture and build-vs-buy decisions, integration into our compute platform, and operating the system in production.

    According to recent reports, your first goal is raw Postgres I/O performance at scale. In the longer term, the layer you build will provide the block-level snapshots and copy-on-write clones behind database branching, fast restores, and instant resizes. Because it's software-defined, it will also travel with us as we expand beyond a single cloud provider into multi-cloud and colocated infrastructure.

    Sources indicate that this is a foundational, high-ownership role. You'll set the technical direction for storage at Supabase and help grow the team around it.

    Lead the architecture of Supabase's NVMe-oF storage platform, including evaluating and deciding between adopting existing software-defined storage and building on SPDK.

    Integrate networked block storage into our Kubernetes-based compute platform through CSI drivers and custom controllers, covering provisioning, attach/detach, resizing, and migration.

    Make Postgres fast on networked storage by profiling and tuning the full I/O path, from fsync, WAL, and checkpoints through the kernel block layer, NVMe/TCP, and the network.

    Design for durability and availability, including replication or erasure coding, failure domains, failover, and data-integrity verification.

    Build I/O isolation and QoS so that noisy neighbors can't degrade other tenants.

    Set performance and reliability SLOs, and build the benchmarking and observability to hold the system to them.

    Design the layer for block-level snapshots and copy-on-write clones, laying the groundwork for database branching.

    Keep the platform portable across AWS, other clouds, and bare-metal/colo.

    Write design docs, mentor engineers, and work closely with the Compute, Branching, Postgres, and Multicloud teams.

    Participate in on-call rotations, incident response, and post-incident reviews.

    Resolve escalated support problems, while also identifying and resolving systemic issues across the platform.

    Have 7+ years of software engineering experience, including significant time building and operating storage systems in production.

    Have built or operated distributed or software-defined block storage (for example Ceph RBD, Lightbits, Simplyblock, Portworx, LINSTOR/DRBD, or an in-house system).

    Have hands-on experience with NVMe/TCP or NVMe-oF, including targets, initiators, multipath, and failover behavior.

    Have a deep understanding of Linux storage internals: the block layer, io_uring, page cache, O_DIRECT and fsync semantics, filesystems, and device-mapper.

    Write strong systems code in Go, plus C, C++, or Rust.

    Measure performance rigorously with fio, pgbench, eBPF, and perf, and can explain latency down to its individual components.

    Understand durability tradeoffs between replication, erasure coding, and consistency under failure.

    Have led technical direction on a complex system: design docs, tradeoffs, and bringing others along.

    Have experience with Kubernetes controllers and/or CSI drivers.

    Have been on call for large production systems.

    Communicate clearly in writing and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Experience implementing block-level snapshots, thin provisioning, or copy-on-write cloning.

    Postgres internals knowledge (WAL, buffer manager, checkpointer), or familiarity with OrioleDB.

    Experience with AWS networking and instance storage at scale (ENA, placement, bandwidth limits).

    Experience running storage on bare metal or in colo.

    Contributions to open source storage projects or the Linux kernel storage stack.

    Sources indicate that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    In a recent development, every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a upcoming city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    According to recent reports, we’re looking for a Software Engineer, Postgres Tooling to join our CLI team and help build the open-source tools developers use to change their Postgres schemas safely. You’ll join as a co-maintainer of pg-delta, our schema diff and migration engine, and grow into leading it.

    Given two databases, or a database and a folder of SQL files describing the schema you want, pg-delta works out the differences and generates the migration to get from one to the other. It powers supabase db diff, db pull, and declarative schemas, and it runs underneath Supabase’s platform, branching, and AI agent workflows. Every migration it generates is verified on a throwaway clone before it’s trusted, and it’s tested against 331 scenarios on PostgreSQL 14–18. We’re now working toward a stable, standalone 1.0 release for any Postgres developer, on Supabase or not.

    According to recent reports, this is a correctness-first role. The SQL this tool generates runs against production databases, so privilege safety and avoiding data loss are non-negotiable. It’s a great fit for someone who loves Postgres at the catalog level, enjoys compiler-style problems, and thrives in async, fast-paced environments.

    Co-maintain pg-delta: review and merge changes, including PRs written by AI agents, and grow into its lead maintainer.

    Own correctness: triage bug reports from GitHub and support, fix diff and dependency-ordering bugs, and extend test coverage across Postgres versions.

    Make sure generated migrations are privilege-safe and never silently lose data, by detecting destructive changes and rewriting them into safe equivalents where possible.

    Help take pg-delta to a stable 1.0: a public API with a semver contract, documentation, and broader coverage of Postgres extensions.

    Work with the open-source community: triage complications, review outside contributions, and say no gracefully when a request doesn’t fit.

    Work with the teams across Supabase that build on pg-delta, so migrations are generated and run the same way everywhere.

    Write the design docs and technical strategy that set the tool’s direction, working async across teams.

    Share the CLI team’s on-call rotation. Weekdays are covered follow-the-sun, and because we ship packaged software that users can roll back, pages are rare.

    Have 8+ years of experience as a software engineer, including deep, hands-on work with PostgreSQL.

    Know Postgres internals at the catalog level: pg_catalog, pg_depend, object ownership, grants and default privileges, RLS policies, and extension membership.

    Understand DDL and migration semantics: which changes take locks, which can’t run inside a transaction, how dependencies determine ordering, and how to spot a destructive change.

    Treat a migration that silently loosens access as a top-severity bug.

    Write strong TypeScript, and design tests for correctness, such as differential, property-based, or corpus testing across multiple Postgres versions.

    Are comfortable with compiler-style problems: dependency graphs, topological ordering, cycle handling, and diffing.

    Can confidently review complex changes in an intricate codebase, including AI-generated PRs.

    Have owned software in production with users in the loop: staged rollouts, error monitoring, and triaging real bug reports.

    Have led a technical project across several teams, from an ambiguous start to production.

    Communicate clearly in writing and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Nice to have, roughly in order of how much they’d help:.

    Have built or maintained schema diff or migration tooling (such as migra, pg-schema-diff, Atlas, pgroll, sqitch, Prisma Migrate, or Flyway/Liquibase), or worked with pg_dump internals.

    Open-source maintainer experience: API contracts, semver, documentation, and community triage.

    Familiarity with Postgres extensions such as pg_cron, pgmq, pg_partman, vault, pg_net, pgvector, or PostGIS.

    Contributions to Postgres itself, or authorship of a Postgres extension.

    Experience with Supabase or another managed Postgres platform.

    Claude Intros Sonnet 5.5 with Model-Switching Cybersecurity Safeguards

    📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthropic's fresh Claude release, Sonnet 5.5, brings cybersecurity safeguards that can change which model handles a request during a Claude conversation.
    • Recent findings suggest that according to Anthropic's explanation of model switching, automatic fallback is enabled by default in Claude.
    • The organization identifies penetration testing and exploit generation among activities that may trigger cybersecurity fallbacks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Anthropic's fresh Claude release, Sonnet 5.5, brings cybersecurity safeguards that can change which model handles a request during a Claude conversation. Higher-risk tasks can fall back to Sonnet 5.

    Recent findings suggest that according to Anthropic's explanation of model switching, automatic fallback is enabled by default in Claude. Users receive a notice, and the answer is labeled with the model that provided it. The chat then stays on Sonnet 5 unless the user changes the selection.

    The organization identifies penetration testing and exploit generation among activities that may trigger cybersecurity fallbacks. Source-code vulnerability scanning remains supported. Biology and reasoning-extraction safeguards can block requests outright, rather than route them elsewhere.

    Sources indicate that the distinction matters operationally. A block stops the request; a fallback allows an attempt to continue with a different model. Neither outcome should be treated as interchangeable with completion by the model the user originally chose.

    Recent findings suggest that anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 generates output more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and can reduce cost per task by up to 30%, based on its testing. Token prices remain unchanged.

    Those claims describe performance under the tech giant's test conditions. An organization evaluating the service also needs to examine what happens when its own assignments encounter safeguards.

    Industry observers note that an internal pilot could record how often work is interrupted, whether fallback answers are usable, and when owners need help. Such measurements would give buyers a more relevant basis for deployment than assuming every task receives the advertised model's capabilities.

    Convergence of AI, Quantum Risks Is Impacting Cybersecurity

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures.
    • The research, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global, examines both the risks and potential benefits of the technologies.
    • Cloud-based storage, cloud-delivered applications, and cloud management infrastructure were the three most frequently cited asset types targeted by attackers, at 35%, 34%, and 32%, respectively.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures. The 2026 Thales Data Threat Report: Quantum & AI Trends, based on responses from 3,120 security and IT management professionals across 20 countries, found that 98% are considering how the two technologies affect each other. Thirty percent reported a significant increase in security budgets specifically for AI.

    The research, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global, examines both the risks and potential benefits of the technologies. Fifty-seven percent believe quantum computing will enhance machine learning, while 54% expect it to enable advanced simulations of complex systems. The security findings span data governance, cloud infrastructure, and preparations for quantum-resistant encryption.

    Cloud-based storage, cloud-delivered applications, and cloud management infrastructure were the three most frequently cited asset types targeted by attackers, at 35%, 34%, and 32%, respectively. The report connects that exposure to the large datasets required for AI training and the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

    In a recent development, organizations are also looking to cloud providers for protection: 67% reported investing in their cloud provider's AI-specific security tools, compared with 63% using an established security provider. Respondents could identify multiple sources of protection, including startups, large language model providers, and internally developed controls.

    Encryption coverage remains incomplete. Only 7% of organizations reported encrypting more than 80% of their sensitive cloud data, while 29% reported encrypting more than 60%. The report's chart puts the average share encrypted at 47% in 2026, down from 51% in 2025.

    Sources indicate that the findings extend concerns raised in coverage of Thales' 2025 cloud security research, when AI security already ranked second to cloud security in spending priorities and 52% of respondents reported that AI security spending was displacing existing security budgets. The latest report again places AI security second, while its historical comparison shows average sensitive cloud data encryption coverage falling from 51% in 2025 to 47% in 2026.

    According to recent reports, AI security was the second-highest prioritized security spending category overall, behind cloud security. But protecting data ranked much lower among the measures organizations use to judge AI projects: Reducing or managing risks of data loss or noncompliance placed sixth among seven success criteria, at 35%.

    Improving customer experience led those measures at 68%, followed by reducing employee toil through greater task automation at 63%. Meanwhile, poor data quality or initial data governance was the leading inhibitor to AI adoption, cited by 65%; security risks from exposed data followed at 61%. Another 51% cited AI initiatives moving too quickly to be properly secured.

    As an umbrella term, education technology encompasses everything from learning management systems and student information systems to productivity tools and AI platforms. More specific language clarifying the difference between ed tech and consumer-facing tools would allow state leaders to match the right evidence, expertise, and policy to the right questions.

    Cybersecurity companies Rubrik and CrowdStrike have announced an expanded identity-security integration designed to move compromised identity environments from threat detection through clean recovery with less manual intervention.

    While security teams have invested heavily in e-mail protection, endpoint security, and identity controls, latest research from Fortra suggests one challenge remains difficult to solve: users.

    Recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures.

    Industry News: Flashpoint Receives Patent for Ransomware Risk Model, Tying Vulnerabilites to Likelihood of Attack

    📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Cybersecurity manufacturer Flashpoint announced it has received U.S.
    • The patent comes at a time when security teams are confronting a growing vulnerability problem: Flashpoint's Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition tracked 21,667 vulnerability disclosures during the first half of 2026, an 8% increase.
    • Of those, 4,015, or around 19 percent, already had public or functional exploit code.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Cybersecurity manufacturer Flashpoint announced it has received U.S. Patent No. 12,705,360 for its Ransomware Risk model, a methodology designed to help security teams determine which newly disclosed vulnerabilities more closely resemble those historically used in ransomware attacks.

    The patent comes at a time when security teams are confronting a growing vulnerability problem: Flashpoint's Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition tracked 21,667 vulnerability disclosures during the first half of 2026, an 8% increase.

    Of those, 4,015, or around 19 percent, already had public or functional exploit code. Flashpoint also reported a 45 percent increase in Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) attacks during the period.

    Sources indicate that the patent was granted August 11 2026, although the underlying Ransomware Risk model isn't upcoming. It has been available through Flashpoint Vulnerability Intelligence since 2022.

    The model addresses a basic vulnerability-management problem: severity and real-world ransomware risk aren't necessarily the same thing, because severity scores do not necessarily indicate which flaws attackers are most likely to target.

    The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, or CVSS, measures how severe a vulnerability could be. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System, or EPSS, estimates the probability of exploitation more broadly.

    Flashpoint's Ransomware Risk model adds another dimension by comparing newly disclosed vulnerabilities with the characteristics of flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks.

    Recent findings suggest that that could change where a vulnerability lands in an organization's patching queue. A lower-severity flaw might normally sit behind numerous critical vulnerabilities. But if its characteristics closely resemble vulnerabilities repeatedly targeted by ransomware operators, security teams may have reason to move it higher.

    Industry observers note that "A severity score alone can't tell you which vulnerabilities pose the greatest real-world risk of exploitation by ransomware actors," Flashpoint CEO Josh Lefkowitz said. "Our patented Ransomware Risk model applies years of threat intelligence to that problem, giving customers an earlier signal and helping them prioritize based on how attackers actually operate.".

    In a recent development, the firm's midyear research also illustrates the scale of the prioritization problem. Its vulnerability intelligence covers traditional IT systems as well as cloud, IoT, operational technology, open source software. and third-party libraries.

    The company says it also tracks more than 105,000 vulnerabilities that aren't represented in CVE or the National Vulnerability Database, expanding the pool of flaws that security teams may need to evaluate.

    The cybersecurity organization's patented methodology profiles vulnerabilities using more than 60 technical characteristics, including whether a flaw can be exploited remotely without authentication, whether it affects operational technology systems, and how exploitation could affect data availability.

    Recent findings suggest that those characteristics form a multi-factor fingerprint. The model maps each vulnerability against clusters containing flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks and assigns a Low, Medium, High, or Critical Ransomware Risk rating.

    Industry observers note that flashpoint says the rating can be generated when a vulnerability is disclosed, rather than requiring security teams to wait for public evidence of active exploitation. Ratings are then updated as upcoming ransomware activity and threat intelligence emerge.

    Within Flashpoint Ignite, Ransomware Risk appears alongside CVSS, EPSS, Social Risk, and exploit maturity. The idea isn't to replace existing scoring systems, but to give administrators additional information when deciding what to remediate first.

    Sources indicate that nor does a High or Critical Ransomware Risk rating mean a vulnerability will necessarily be exploited. The model measures how closely its characteristics resemble vulnerabilities historically associated with ransomware attacks.

    Sources indicate that for security teams facing thousands of potential vulnerabilities, that distinction matters. The flaw carrying the highest severity score isn't necessarily the one that most closely resembles what ransomware operators have historically chosen to attack.

    "Despite being the most popular indicator for priority, we know that severity alone doesn't tell you whether a vulnerability will be exploited or used in ransomware," said Ben Haynes, Data Science & Analytics Lead at Flashpoint and co-inventor of the patented methodology.

    "A vulnerability can score low on a traditional severity scale and still share the characteristics we repeatedly see in ransomware attacks.".

    For more information, go to the Flashpoint site.

    SailPoint Intros New Capabilities to Address Agentic AI Identity Security Challenge

    📅 12 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security tech giant SailPoint.
    • That gap could become harder to ignore as organizations give agents more autonomy.
    • Industry observers note that sailPoint, which develops identity security and access governance technology for enterprises, is responding with a collection of new identity security capabilities confirmed at its Navigate 2026 conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security tech giant SailPoint. In its latest Horizons of Identity Security report, SailPoint found that 79% of enterprises already have AI agents running in production, while just 2% have deployed identity security tools specifically designed to govern them.

    That gap could become harder to ignore as organizations give agents more autonomy. Agents can increasingly access applications, sensitive data, and credentials, and in some cases take actions on a user's behalf, effectively creating a new class of identity that IT and security teams need to manage.

    Industry observers note that sailPoint, which develops identity security and access governance technology for enterprises, is responding with a collection of new identity security capabilities confirmed at its Navigate 2026 conference. The company is expanding its Agentic Fabric to discover "shadow AI" agents and provide runtime authorization and controls capable of immediately disabling an agent.

    According to recent reports, the manufacturer also introduced what it calls SailPoint Autonomous Agents, specialized AI agents designed to govern other agents. The security agents can monitor runtime activity, intercept threats, and adjust permissions while allowing legitimate agents to continue operating, SailPoint said.

    The idea reflects one of the challenges created by increasingly autonomous AI systems: Traditional human approval processes may not be fast enough to govern software capable of taking large numbers of actions on its own.

    "The idea that a security admin is going to review and approve access for a group of autonomous agents making 10,000 tool calls a second isn't just outdated — it's a fantasy," SailPoint CTO Chandra Gnanasambandam said.

    Another part of SailPoint's approach focuses on visibility.

    Latest endpoint and browser sensors, along with SIEM and XDR telemetry and non-human identity discovery capabilities, are designed to uncover agents, MCP servers, credentials, tools, and data stores that haven't been brought under an organization's identity program.

    The company is also introducing Autonomous Identity Security Posture Management, or A-ISPM, which uses identity information from its Atlas platform to identify dormant accounts, orphaned access, shadow administrators, and other potentially risky access paths. Organizations can then revoke access, disable an identity or AI agent, assign an owner or automate enforcement.

    Just-in-Time provisioning is another part of the strategy. Rather than giving people, service accounts, and AI agents permanent access, permissions can be granted when needed and subjected to conditions such as reauthentication or a business justification.

    Recent findings suggest that capabilities across SailPoint's Agentic Fabric, Human Fabric, and Atlas platforms are beginning to roll out globally. A-ISPM and several other announced features are expected in the company's fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.

    "Autonomous agents are no longer just experimental copilots; they are becoming the primary execution layer of modern enterprises," SailPoint President Matt Mills remarked.

    For more information, go to the SailPoint site.

    As schools become more dependent on digital platforms for instruction, grading, student services, and family communication, resilience depends not only on preventing attacks, but on how quickly leaders can restore trusted data, recover essential services, and keep disruptions from cascading across the school community.

    Increasingly, cyber criminals are sharing AI prompts, jailbreak techniques, and access to existing models that can be incorporated into fraud and phishing operations, according the latest AI Threat Report from Flashpoint.

    NVIDIA and 36 other industry partners are targeting agent security across multi-vendor clouds by combining open technologies for workload identity, agent controls, vulnerability scanning, and software supply-chain security.

    According to a survey by data and AI services provider Further, enterprises are reporting benefits from artificial intelligence even as their data preparation and oversight processes remain incomplete.
